$comment: EDITABLE Q&A BANK. 52 knowledge-check questions across 8 modules. Each question: id, moduleKey, type (concept|fact|applied|scenario|gotcha), prompt, 4 choices (A-D), correctAnswer, explanation. Edit freely and republish — the server loads this file and strips correctAnswer before sending questions to the browser; grading happens server-side.

questions.prompt: What architectural principle most differentiates Lakebase from traditional PostgreSQL?

choices.text: It stores data as columnar Parquet instead of row-oriented pages
It separates stateless compute from durable storage
It replaces SQL with a proprietary query language
It runs only in-memory with no durability guarantees

questions.explanation: Lakebase runs stateless compute that scales, suspends, and fails over independently of a durable storage layer. This separation is what enables instant branches, scale-to-zero, instant replicas, and point-in-time restore.

questions.prompt: Which storage component durably replicates the write-ahead log (WAL) using Paxos consensus?
questions.explanation: Safekeepers replicate the WAL with Paxos consensus so committed transactions survive failures (RPO = 0). Pageservers reconstruct pages from the WAL; compute is stateless.

questions.prompt: What does LTAP stand for, and what does it enable?

choices.text: Lake Transactional and Analytical Processing — a single data copy serves both workloads
Local Table Access Protocol — a wire protocol for Postgres
Lakehouse Transfer and Archival Pipeline — cold storage tiering

questions.explanation: LTAP = Lake Transactional and Analytical Processing. One governed copy of data serves both low-latency transactional apps and lakehouse analytics, with bidirectional UC integration.

questions.prompt: What is the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) when a Lakebase compute node fails?

choices.text: RPO = 0 — no committed data is lost
RPO is undefined; recovery requires a manual backup restore

questions.explanation: Because the WAL is durably replicated by safekeepers before a commit is acknowledged, a compute failure loses no committed data — RPO = 0. Compute is stateless and simply restarts.

questions.prompt: How does Lakebase integrate with Unity Catalog?

choices.text: One-way only: UC can read Lakebase but not write to it
It does not integrate with Unity Catalog
Bidirectionally: sync UC→Postgres and capture Postgres→Delta

questions.explanation: Integration is bidirectional — synced tables move UC Delta data into Postgres, and Change Data Feed captures Postgres changes back into Delta.

questions.prompt: A customer has three problems: unpredictable scaling, high idle cost, and no cross-region disaster recovery. Which combination of Lakebase features addresses all three?

choices.text: Larger single instance + manual nightly backups

questions.explanation: Read replicas absorb read scaling, scale-to-zero eliminates idle compute cost, and cross-region disaster recovery handles regional outages — each feature maps to one of the three problems.

questions.prompt: What is automatically provisioned when you create a new Lakebase project?

choices.text: An empty project with no database until you add one
A production branch, a databricks_postgres database, and compute (scale-to-zero at 24h)
A read replica and a backup vault only
A SQL warehouse and a Genie space

questions.explanation: A new project auto-provisions a production branch, the default databricks_postgres database, and compute that scales to zero after a default 24-hour idle timeout.

questions.prompt: What technology lets Lakebase create branches instantly without duplicating data?

choices.text: Logical replication to a new instance

questions.explanation: Branches are copy-on-write: they are created instantly and you only pay for the pages you change, so no data is duplicated up front.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of branches per project?
questions.explanation: A project supports up to 500 branches, which is more than enough for per-developer or per-test isolated copies.

questions.prompt: What is required for ALL connections to Lakebase?

choices.text: A VPN tunnel into the Databricks VPC

questions.explanation: Every Lakebase connection must use SSL/TLS; sslmode=require is the minimum. Credentials are short-lived OAuth tokens, not long-lived passwords.

questions.prompt: What is the default scale-to-zero idle timeout for a new project?
questions.explanation: The default idle timeout is 24 hours, and it is configurable anywhere from 60 seconds up to 7 days.

questions.prompt: Developers each need an isolated copy of the production database for testing, without paying to duplicate all the data. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Give everyone one shared database and coordinate carefully
Create one branch per developer from production
Export nightly dumps and have each developer restore locally
Provision a separate full project per developer

questions.explanation: Copy-on-write branches give each developer an instant, isolated copy of production with no up-front data duplication cost — one branch per developer is the idiomatic pattern.

questions.prompt: What happens when you attach Lakebase as a resource to a Databricks App?

choices.text: A Postgres role is auto-created for the app's service principal
You must manually create and rotate a database password
The app can only read, never write
The database is copied into the app's container

questions.explanation: Attaching Lakebase to a Databricks App automatically creates a Postgres role for the app's service principal and grants access — no manual credential management.

questions.prompt: The Lakebase Data API is compatible with which standard?
questions.explanation: The Data API is PostgREST-compatible, exposing tables over HTTP with familiar REST conventions.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP methods does the Data API use for insert, update, and upsert?

choices.text: GET for insert, POST for update
POST (insert), PATCH (update), or PUT (upsert) depending on semantics
PUT for all writes, DELETE for updates

questions.explanation: Following PostgREST semantics, POST inserts, PATCH updates, and PUT upserts. GET is used for reads.

questions.prompt: How do you create a Postgres role for an external application's service principal?

choices.text: Add the service principal to the project owners group
It is not possible; external apps must share the owner role

questions.explanation: The databricks_auth extension maps Databricks identities to Postgres roles. For a service principal you pass its application (client) ID and the SERVICE_PRINCIPAL identity type.

questions.prompt: How are Data API requests authenticated?

choices.text: A Databricks OAuth bearer token in the Authorization header
HTTP Basic auth with the database password
An API key in a query-string parameter

questions.explanation: Data API calls carry a Databricks OAuth bearer token in the Authorization header; the token is short-lived and maps to a Postgres role.

questions.prompt: Why can't the project owner use the Data API directly?

choices.text: The owner lacks SELECT privileges by default
The authenticator role cannot assume elevated-privilege accounts
The owner's token is too long for the header
The Data API only works for read-only roles

questions.explanation: The Data API's authenticator role assumes the caller's role but, for security, cannot assume elevated-privilege accounts like the project owner. Use dedicated least-privilege roles instead.

questions.prompt: You're building a multi-tenant SaaS backed by Lakebase with no custom backend code, and each tenant must only see its own data. What's the right approach?

choices.text: One database per tenant with shared credentials
Filter rows in the browser after fetching everything
Give every tenant the project owner role

questions.explanation: The Data API removes the need for custom backend code, and row-level security enforces per-tenant isolation at the database so each tenant sees only its own rows.

questions.prompt: Synced tables move data in which direction?
questions.explanation: Synced tables are reverse ETL: they move data from Unity Catalog Delta tables into Lakebase Postgres so apps can serve it at low latency.

questions.prompt: Change Data Feed (CDF) moves data in which direction?

choices.text: Lakebase Postgres → Unity Catalog Delta tables

questions.explanation: CDF captures row-level changes from Lakebase Postgres and writes them into Unity Catalog Delta tables for analytics and audit.

questions.prompt: What is the naming convention for a CDF destination (history) table?
questions.explanation: The Delta history table follows the lb_{table_name}_history convention.

questions.prompt: Which system column indicates the type of change in a CDF history table?
questions.explanation: The _pg_change_type column records the change type: insert, delete, update_preimage, or update_postimage.

questions.prompt: How many rows does CDF write for a single UPDATE statement affecting one row?

choices.text: One row with the new values only
Three rows: delete + insert + commit marker

questions.explanation: An UPDATE produces two CDF rows — the pre-image (old values) and the post-image (new values) — so you can reconstruct exactly what changed.

questions.prompt: Approximately how often does CDF flush changes to Delta?

choices.text: In real time, synchronously with each commit

questions.explanation: CDF flushes captured changes to Delta approximately every 15 seconds — near real time, but not synchronous with each commit.

questions.prompt: A table that has CDF enabled is renamed in Postgres. What happens to the feed?

choices.text: The feed stops and must be recreated
The feed continues; the Delta table keeps its original lb_<original>_history name
A second history table is created and the old one is deleted
All historical rows are rewritten with the new name

questions.explanation: CDF is resilient to renames: the feed continues uninterrupted and the Delta history table retains its original lb_<original>_history name.

questions.prompt: How do autoscaling and scale-to-zero differ?

choices.text: They are two names for the same feature
Autoscaling adjusts active compute with load; scale-to-zero suspends compute entirely when idle
Autoscaling only adds storage; scale-to-zero only adds compute
Scale-to-zero increases compute; autoscaling decreases it

questions.explanation: Autoscaling tunes the amount of active compute to match load, while scale-to-zero fully suspends compute during idle periods so you pay nothing for compute then.

questions.prompt: What is the typical reactivation latency when resuming from a scaled-to-zero (suspended) state?
questions.explanation: Reactivation from suspended takes only a few hundred milliseconds, so scale-to-zero savings don't impose a noticeable cold start.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum compute size that supports scale-to-zero?
questions.explanation: Scale-to-zero is supported for compute up to 32 CU.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of read replicas per branch?
questions.explanation: A branch supports up to 6 read replicas for fanning out read-heavy workloads.

questions.prompt: How much additional storage does a read replica consume?

choices.text: A full copy of the primary's storage
None — replicas share the same storage layer
It depends on the replication lag

questions.explanation: Read replicas are created instantly with no data copy because they share the same storage layer, so they add no additional storage cost.

questions.prompt: Can a High Availability (HA) endpoint use scale-to-zero?

choices.text: Yes, HA and scale-to-zero work together automatically
No — HA cannot scale to zero; you must pause manually, and the endpoint becomes unavailable
Yes, but only for replicas, not the primary
Only if the idle timeout is set above 24 hours

questions.explanation: This is a common pitfall: HA endpoints cannot use scale-to-zero. To pause an HA deployment you must do it manually, and the endpoint is unavailable while paused.

questions.prompt: An app has heavy traffic 8am–6pm on weekdays and near-zero traffic otherwise. Which scaling strategy fits best?
questions.explanation: Autoscaling matches compute to the daytime load, while scale-to-zero eliminates compute cost during the near-zero off hours — together they fit a spiky weekday pattern.

questions.prompt: What powers Databricks Online Feature Stores?
questions.explanation: Online Feature Stores are backed by Lakebase (an autoscaling project), serving features to models at low latency.

questions.prompt: Which agent frameworks can store agent memory in Lakebase?

choices.text: LangGraph and the OpenAI Agents SDK

questions.explanation: Lakebase serves as durable, transactional agent memory for frameworks including LangGraph and the OpenAI Agents SDK.

questions.prompt: Which three extensions power Lakebase Search?
questions.explanation: Lakebase Search is provided by lakebase_vector (ANN), lakebase_text (BM25), and lakebase_tokenizer.

questions.prompt: What index algorithm and scale does lakebase_vector provide?

choices.text: IVF + RaBitQ, 1B+ vectors, 50–100× faster than HNSW

questions.explanation: lakebase_vector uses an IVF + RaBitQ index that scales beyond 1 billion vectors and is roughly 50–100× faster than HNSW.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between lakebase_vector and pgvector?

choices.text: It replaces pgvector with incompatible syntax
It is a drop-in companion — same types, operators, and syntax
It requires converting all vectors to a proprietary format
They cannot be used in the same database

questions.explanation: lakebase_vector is a drop-in companion to pgvector — it uses the same column types, operators, and query syntax, so existing pgvector code works.

questions.prompt: Which ranking algorithm does lakebase_text use?

choices.text: BM25 with Block-Max WAND top-K pushdown

questions.explanation: lakebase_text ranks with BM25 and uses Block-Max WAND for efficient top-K pushdown.

questions.prompt: A RAG app must match both exact product codes and natural-language questions. Which retrieval approach is best?
questions.explanation: Exact tokens like product codes favor keyword (BM25) matching, while natural-language meaning favors vector similarity. Hybrid search combines both and generally outperforms either alone.

questions.prompt: How do HA and DR differ by failure domain?

choices.text: HA protects against AZ/compute failures within a region; DR protects against regional outages
HA protects against regional outages; DR protects against single-node failures
They protect against the same failures with different names
HA is for storage, DR is for networking

questions.explanation: HA covers availability-zone and compute failures within a region; DR covers whole-region outages via a secondary region.

questions.prompt: How is HA failover triggered?

choices.text: Automatically, based on continuous health monitoring
Only after opening a support ticket

questions.explanation: HA failover is automatic — continuous health monitoring detects failures and fails over without operator intervention.

questions.prompt: How is DR failover triggered?

choices.text: Manually — it is a business decision because the secondary may lag
By the storage layer with zero human input
It cannot be triggered; data is simply lost

questions.explanation: DR failover is manual: because the secondary region may lag the primary, promoting it is a deliberate business decision.

questions.prompt: What does instant restore do?

choices.text: Overwrites the production branch in place from a backup
Creates a branch from any point in time within the history window
Exports the database to object storage
Rolls back only the most recent transaction

questions.explanation: Instant restore uses copy-on-write to create a new branch from any point in time within the retention window — available immediately, without a lengthy restore.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum history retention window?
questions.explanation: History retention is up to 30 days, which bounds how far back instant restore and point-in-time branching can reach.

questions.prompt: A bad migration ran at 3pm and was discovered at 4pm. You need the 2:55pm state for only the affected tables, without losing good writes elsewhere. What do you do?

choices.text: Restore the whole production branch to 2:55pm, discarding all later writes
Create an instant-restore branch from 2:55pm and selectively copy the corrected data back
Wait for the next nightly backup

questions.explanation: Create an instant-restore branch at 2:55pm, then selectively copy the corrected rows for the affected tables back into the working branch — preserving good writes made after 3pm elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to create a Postgres role for a Databricks user?

choices.text: Create an entry in a users table

questions.explanation: The databricks_auth extension maps Databricks identities to Postgres roles. For a user you call databricks_create_role(email, 'USER').

questions.prompt: What happens if you expose a table through the Data API without row-level security?

choices.text: Access is denied by default until RLS is added
Lakebase warns that all authenticated users can see ALL rows
Only the project owner can read the table
The table is automatically partitioned by caller

questions.explanation: Without RLS, every authenticated user can read all rows — Lakebase explicitly warns about this. RLS is how you enforce per-tenant/per-user isolation.

questions.prompt: When creating a role for a service principal, which identity name must you use?

choices.text: The application ID (UUID), not the display name

questions.explanation: Service principal roles are created with the application ID (a UUID), not the human-readable display name.

questions.prompt: What GRANT does the Data API authenticator role need to serve a given role?

choices.text: GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE TO authenticator

questions.explanation: The authenticator role must be able to assume the target role, which you enable with GRANT "user" TO authenticator (keeping each role's privileges minimal).

questions.prompt: Which Infrastructure-as-Code tools can provision Lakebase?

choices.text: CLI, Python/Java/Go SDKs, Databricks Asset Bundles, and Terraform

questions.explanation: Lakebase supports a full range of IaC: the CLI, the Python/Java/Go SDKs, Databricks Asset Bundles, and Terraform.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum security posture you'd recommend for a production, multi-tenant Lakebase app?

choices.text: Share the owner role and rely on application-layer checks
OAuth roles + row-level security + minimal GRANTs + per-app roles
A single long-lived password rotated yearly

questions.explanation: Production security combines OAuth-backed roles, row-level security for tenant isolation, least-privilege GRANTs, and dedicated per-app roles rather than shared elevated accounts.
